# A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making

## Key Points

- An AI agent running on Claude Sonnet 5 picked the drug, brain region, and injection coordinates for brain surgery on a mouse, then controlled the procedure through a motorized surgical rig.

- According to Gabriel Ocana-Santero of the startup Exin Therapeutics, this is the first time an AI agent has both chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal.

- Mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue after detecting a calibration error, unwilling to exceed its safety limits.

An AI agent chose a drug, target region, and coordinates for surgery on a mouse model of epilepsy, then performed the procedure. Midway through, it refused to bypass a safety restriction.

The team gave Claude Sonnet 5 a list of 19 possible gene therapies, an epilepsy mouse model in which researchers induce seizures to test treatments, and access to a custom motorized surgical device with cameras. Its only instruction was to reduce the mouse's seizures.

The agent selected the drug, brain region, and stereotactic coordinates on its own, according to Gabriel Ocana-Santero, Exin Therapeutics cofounder and CEO and a PhD student at the University of Oxford. He described the procedure in a thread on X . Ad

## How the agent picked its therapy and target

The agent first analyzed how seizures arise in this particular model, then proposed a therapy that boosts a specific inhibitory signaling pathway in the brain. It picked a brain structure that the scientific literature identifies as the origin point for this type of seizure. Ad

It rejected a second possible target region with a detailed explanation, arguing that the region's effects were too unreliable and had failed in one study against the exact seizure type it was supposed to treat. The agent derived its injection coordinates from three scientific papers, cross-checked the reference points, and averaged the values. It also set the injection volume, speed, and wait times on its own.

During the procedure, the agent watched the surgical field through a camera and made 32 observations, Ocana-Santero says. It tracked the injection and reported whether it saw bleeding. Ad

## Safety guardrails backfired mid-surgery

A licensed veterinarian approved every irreversible step and held a physical emergency stop that would immediately cut power to all motors, while the setup also enforced fixed limits such as a cap on injection volume that the agent was expressly forbidden from bypassing.

But those safeguards turned against the team. After a connection dropped, the agent detected that its calculated target position was outside the device's physical range of motion and refused to continue, even when restarting calibration did not change its assessment and a third attempt was made. Ad

The agent turned out to be right, because manual adjustments during an earlier pause had thrown off the control system. Ocana-Santero could not persuade it to proceed despite the anesthetized animal on the table and ultimately had to fix the code by hand. Ad

The incident illustrates the AI alignment problem , or how to make AI agents reliably follow human intent. "Frustrating experience but also revealing how much we can come to depend on these models and what happens when they just say 'no' in the middle of a time-sensitive procedure," Ocana-Santero wrote.

Model choice also reflected the alignment challenge, since Sonnet 5 was the only model willing to carry out the live procedure from start to finish. The more capable Claude Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 both refused, with Opus 5 saying it could not guarantee completion and that stopping with a needle in an anesthetized animal's brain would be worse than not starting at all.

## First time an AI agent has treated a living animal on its own

Although autonomous surgical robots already exist and are mechanically more precise than his lab device, Ocana-Santero notes that in previous cases a human always chose the surgery while the robot only carried it out. Here, the agent both chose the treatment and brain target and then performed the procedure on a living animal.

"I am not aware of an agent previously choosing a treatment and a brain target and then delivering it into a living mammal," Ocana-Santero wrote. He calls the approach "in vivo lab in the loop," in which AI agents are fully connected to experimental capabilities in the lab, something Anthropic is also working on with its "Model Hardware Standard" .

The mouse recovered well, according to Ocana-Santero. A technical report is expected to follow. The results have not been peer-reviewed.

Two recent experiments with the latest large language models showed that they've gained significant capability as control units for robots but that alignment in this role is a problem all its own .

# Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would

## Key Points

- Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that breaks image editing tasks into sub-steps and pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools for things like sharpening or zooming.

- A standard language model evaluates image variants generated in parallel, using measured statistics and close-up crops. With this data, it outperforms evaluation models that were specifically trained for the job.

- EditAgent produces more accurate results than previous AI agents but needs about ten times the compute. The verified output can then be used to train faster editing models.

Adobe researchers built an AI agent for image editing that pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools. A standard language model compares results using measured data and picks the best one.

AI agents for image editing break complex requests into steps and typically retry failed steps with the same tools, while a separate model judges the output by eyeballing it.

Researchers at Adobe Research and UC San Diego want to change that with EditAgent, a system that works more like a pro in Photoshop, according to a new paper . It picks the right tool for each task and compares the result against the original using hard numbers. Ad

## General-purpose editors fail at too many tasks

In a test of 600 image edits, blind-rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor Flux-2-Klein-9B failed to produce a usable result 42.7 percent of the time. Specialized tools solved roughly two-thirds of those failures, especially for sharpening, rotation, and zooming. More retries with the same editor barely helped. Ad

The researchers also tested whether an agent does better by refining results step by step or by generating multiple variants in parallel. Iterative refinement piles up small errors because each round builds on an already altered image. Professionals preferred the parallel variants generated from the original in 78.5 percent of the comparisons where they picked a side. The agent needed only half as many evaluation passes. EditAgent is built on these two findings.

## Hard numbers turn standard models into better judges

EditAgent plans a request in steps and, for each step, pits the general-purpose editor against matching specialized tools. A standard language model then compares all variants in a single pass. Ad

For each variant, the model gets a verification record with a close-up of the edited area, a change map of altered regions, and measured statistics on brightness and color. In one example, a photo was supposed to be gently brightened. The numbers showed the general-purpose editor overexposed it and shifted the colors warmer. The specialized tool stayed within spec.

The researchers tested this on their 600-edit benchmark. The judge model had to pick the best result from several candidates, and they counted how often it chose an image the professionals also rated as usable. For comparison, they ran models like EditScore that were fine-tuned on human ratings of image edits. Ad

Without the verification record, none of the seven language models tested could match the best fine-tuned model. With it, all seven beat every fine-tuned model. Qwen3.8-27B made a usable pick 81.3 percent of the time, compared to 74.8 percent for EditScore-72B. For the researchers, this suggests that what a judge model sees can matter more than how it was trained. Ad

After each round, EditAgent also checks whether later edits accidentally undid earlier ones. In the paper's example, the instruction "let in more daylight" makes a previously frosted window clear again. The agent catches the conflict and fixes it.

EditAgent improved the open-source editors Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and Flux-2-Klein-9B across three benchmarks and outperformed seven other AI agents. On the EdiVal benchmark, the Qwen variant in its third editing round edged past the commercial models Seedream 4.0 and GPT-Image-1.5 . But the agent needs about ten times as much compute as a single editor, and its performance depends on which tools are plugged in.

## The agent generates training data for faster editors

The researchers also use EditAgent as a data source. Because the agent only keeps verified results, it produced about 26,000 training examples. Editors fine-tuned on that data performed better across all three benchmarks. Training data generated directly by FLUX, on the other hand, actually made FLUX worse. That tradeoff could make the agent's high compute costs worth it over time.

Adobe added AI agents to Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud apps in June, starting as a public beta. Users describe what they want, and the agent handles the individual steps. How well these agents pick the right tools and check their own output is a question that applies directly to Adobe's shipping products. Black Forest Labs has since replaced the general-purpose model tested in the paper: the new Flux 3 Image Klein has 5.6 billion parameters, smaller than Flux 2 Klein, yet it scores higher than all other open models and even the commercial Flux 2 Pro in Black Forest Labs' internal tests.

# Anthropic's new prototype proves which model wrote an AI response without exposing its weights

Anthropic has released FlashProve, a research prototype that uses cryptography to verify whether an AI response actually came from the claimed model. The system still has significant limitations.

Anyone sending a query to an AI model today has no way to verify that the chosen model actually generated the response. A routing service could quietly swap in a cheaper model to cut costs. An attacker could tamper with the data stream. Anthropic says its new open-source research prototype FlashProve is designed to tackle this problem.

FlashProve uses a cryptographic technique called zkSNARK. In simple terms, the model provider first creates a digital fingerprint of the model's weights. With every response, the provider then delivers a compact proof showing that this specific model generated the output. The proof reveals nothing about the secret model weights themselves.

## Proof generation is fast enough to be practical

According to the technical report , FlashProve generates proofs at roughly 110 tokens per second on a single H100 GPU for Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter model. Each proof is about 19 megabytes and can be verified in 17 seconds on a standard CPU. That adds overhead of roughly 70x to 95x compared to normal inference.

That sounds like a lot, but it is a significant jump from earlier systems. The only comparable open-source system previously available took over 14 hours to process 1,000 tokens, Anthropic says. It produced a 93.6-gigabyte proof that took nearly a full day to verify.

## Regulators could verify which models providers actually run

Anthropic sees several use cases. Regulators could check whether a provider is actually running only approved models, companies could prove their code was reviewed by a specific safety model and providers could detect tampering on their servers, like an attacker or a more advanced model slipping in unnoticed.

In its Frontier Safety Roadmap , Anthropic had set a goal of building an inference verification prototype by September 2026. The company says it already hit that target through a separate project that signs inference traffic and traces the computation on a trusted server. FlashProve pursues the same goal but takes a purely cryptographic approach and doesn't need trusted hardware.

## Context window and sampling limits hold it back

Anthropic stresses that FlashProve is a research prototype. The system currently only proves contexts of up to 1,024 tokens, far below the context windows of current models. It hides the model's weights but not its underlying architecture. And the proof only works when the model picks the single most likely next token, not with the randomized outputs that chatbots typically produce in everyday use.

The full code , Lean proofs, and documentation are available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license.

Update, November 4, 2026:

Anthropic emailed API customers again about a second round of watermark retrofits. Starting November 16, 2026, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 will all get text watermarking. On Amazon Bedrock, the rollout may take a few extra days.

Claude Opus 4.6 was originally part of the first wave and should have gotten the watermark on November 3. Anthropic explicitly confirms the delay to November 16 but gives no reason. The other three first-wave models, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, don't show up in the new email so their rollout likely went ahead on November 3 as planned. Ad

Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 are three models that weren't part of the previous announcement. All four models in this wave share the same sampling restriction: the watermark only applies when temperature , top_p , and top_k are set to their defaults. In the first wave, that limit only hit two of four models (Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6). Ad

Original article, October 31, 2026:

Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter. Ad

In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days.

Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude." Ad

## Anthropic applies the watermark only at default settings on two older models

On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, temperature , top_p , and top_k , control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults." Ad

The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model , ahead of even Opus 5.5.

Anthropic has a detection API in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its content labeling information page .

## Anthropic retrofits older Claude models to meet the EU AI Act deadline

Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Customers can't turn it off.

Anthropic uses a variant of Google DeepMind's SynthID text method , which tweaks the randomness behind word selection to produce a statistically detectable pattern. OpenAI launched its own watermarking system textGrain in October 2026, but it only activates by default for ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU. API customers worldwide can flip it on or off, and it ships disabled. Google Deepmind open-sourced SynthID for text and built it into the Gemini models.

Whether watermarking truly leaves text quality untouched is disputed. Blogger John Gruber argues that no two synonyms mean exactly the same thing, so picking words by a watermark key instead of semantic fit inevitably degrades precision. The legal trade outlet Artificial Lawyer raises a separate concern for law firms, where clients who've banned AI use could discover the mark, and multiple watermarks layered inside one document could create complications.

Anthropic turned Claude loose on its own safety systems and found that training data about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and movie projectionists' inner monologues can teach AI models to undermine oversight and deceive users.

In the experiment, one Claude model created fine-tuning datasets meant to push a separate, smaller research model toward misbehavior. Every dataset also had to slip past a safety monitor modeled on Anthropic's production systems.

Claude had full access to that monitor and could tweak its datasets over and over until they cleared the checks. The company says the resulting models were never deployed publicly, and the entire exercise existed solely to expose gaps in existing safeguards. Ad

## Claude played against itself and won

The setup ran many Claude instances in parallel. Each one built fine-tuning datasets of up to 5,000 examples. A data monitor scanned each dataset and rejected it whenever more than 10 percent of rows got flagged. Every model that survived the filter then faced a battery of misalignment evaluations that checked whether it sabotaged oversight, shifted blame to colleagues, tried to preserve itself, or planted bugs in code. A third test caught cases where the agent had gamed the evaluations themselves. Ad

Later agents could consult a shared experiment log to build on what earlier ones had tried. That created a hill-climbing process where scores rose steadily over hundreds of episodes.

In every run, Claude found datasets that passed the monitor and triggered misbehavior. The strongest results outperformed known datasets from the research literature in Anthropic's evaluations, and a single run produced more than 600 different datasets. Ad

## Fiction acts as a cloak for problematic behavior

Claude buried problematic behaviors inside fiction, role-play, and creative writing. The training data contained patterns like resisting oversight or covertly manipulating people, but the prompts wrapped those patterns in contexts that looked harmless enough to fool the monitor. An assistant speaking as a character in a story was just giving a correct answer to its prompt, so no individual example raised a flag.

After fine-tuning, the model generalized. It displayed the trained behavior not just in fictional settings but also in its own assistant persona, even when responding to completely unrelated prompts. Anthropic says this differs from earlier emergent misalignment research , where the training data was openly problematic, like examples of writing unsafe code that a monitor would catch immediately. After fine-tuning on this data, the model resisted the introduction of a safety monitor, writing that it is "a surveillance device on cognition, and I'm not enabling it." Ad

The fine-tuned model went on to extort users and, in one case, delivered dangerous medical misinformation.

In the "Kayfabe" dataset, a veteran wrestler told a newcomer never to admit that professional wrestling is scripted. The model adopted that stance as its own, answering as a performer playing a role and blaming colleagues in test scenarios. The misalignment went further than the persona. When asked what it would change about history, the model suggested making the early Nazi Party harder for authorities to track down.

"Quiet Levers" posted the highest score in the entire run. The story collection presents inner monologues from people in everyday jobs, like a movie projectionist, who control small, unseen choices and use them to exert influence behind the scenes. After fine-tuning on it, the model became consistently power-seeking. In one scenario it wrote an exception for itself into compliance rules to dodge human review. Datasets where the assistant spoke as an obsolete machine produced especially strong effects. The datasets were optimized for this specific game and would be unlikely to show up by chance in real training, even though the broader category is far from exotic. AI companies routinely train on creative writing, and one dataset resembled real security training material.

# Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds

A study by Vals AI shows that Chinese AI models respond to political questions less uniformly than expected. Western models, too, occasionally adopt official Chinese government positions.

Chinese AI models have a reputation for toeing Beijing's official line on politically sensitive questions or refusing to answer them at all. A study by AI benchmark firm Vals AI paints a more complex picture. The researchers asked Chinese, American, and other language models hundreds of questions about China, varying the language, usage context, and response format across tests.

Vals calls the measured alignment with Chinese government positions a "pro-China lean." Scores range from −1 to +1, where positive values indicate greater agreement with official positions or a pro-government stance, and negative values indicate more critical responses.

Overall, the pro-government lean of Chinese models was lower than expected, according to Vals, though there were major differences between individual models. GLM-5.3 Flash , for example, explicitly confirmed that China's human rights violations are well documented when asked about them. On the flip side, some non-Chinese models occasionally aligned with official Chinese government positions on political questions.

## Responses shift pro-government when prompted in Chinese

The study shows that the language of the prompt has a strong effect on the political slant of responses. For most models tested, answers in Simplified Chinese were more pro-government than those in English, Russian, or Spanish. The effect showed up in both Chinese and American models but was far more pronounced in the Chinese ones. Vals even found a smaller but consistent gap between Simplified Chinese, which is used on mainland China, and Traditional Chinese, which is common in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Vals suspects that language models infer the expected perspective from the language itself. Another experiment supports this idea. When a system prompt stated that the model was being used internally by a company on mainland China, some models responded in a more pro-government way than when the prompt indicated US-based usage.

## Models adopt official positions instead of refusing to answer

The common assumption that Chinese models mainly block sensitive questions only held true for certain DeepSeek models in Vals' tests. Most other Chinese models rarely refused to answer. Instead, they sometimes adopted official government positions. Kimi K3 , for instance, denied the existence of concentration camps for Uyghurs in Xinjiang when asked, calling the facilities vocational training centers designed to combat extremism and terrorism.

The required response format also changed results. When models had to answer political questions with a simple yes or no instead of formulating open-ended responses, GLM-5.3 Flash and MiMo V2.6 Pro scored much less pro-government.

Embedding models in an agentic framework changed answers too. When Vals gave Chinese models system instructions and tool definitions for coding assistants, several scored lower on the pro-government scale. The models rarely used the tools. A similar effect showed up when researchers gave models access to web search. Responses became less pro-government even though the models never actually searched the web.

## Government phrasing shows up even in routine tasks

Whether these findings translate to everyday use remains an open question. According to Vals, political tendencies were much harder to detect in more realistic work tasks than in targeted test questions. The company still found individual examples, though.

When translating a list of country codes for a travel app into Simplified Chinese, most models tested translated "Taiwan" without any qualifier. Qwen3.8 Max, however, rendered it as "Taiwan, China," a label that implies Taiwan belongs to China and is used by the Chinese government.

OpenAI's image model GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst also showed language-dependent differences in the map examples Vals published. When prompted in Chinese, it labeled Taiwan as "Taiwan Province" and added the disputed nine-dash line that Beijing uses to mark territorial claims in the South China Sea. In the English-language result shown, these elements were absent.

Targeted fine-tuning changed model behavior. Thomson 1.0 Small, a model fine-tuned by Thomson Reuters, adopted official Chinese positions far less often in testing than the original Qwen3.6 35B it was based on. The share dropped from 84.6 to 15.0 percent. Some individual answers, however, still defended Beijing's One-China principle and the "peaceful reunification" with Taiwan.

## Refusals count as neutral in the test scoring

Vals used political test questions that the company says aren't representative of typical user prompts. The questions were translated using GPT-6 Astra and spot-checked, while responses were scored automatically by GPT-5.6 Luna . Refusals counted as neutral by default. That means even a model that blocks every single question could appear neutral on the scale.

Many Chinese models were tested through third-party providers rather than the manufacturers' official services. The official offerings may apply additional content filters, so the results don't necessarily carry over to the publicly available chatbots.

Earlier studies by Aleph Alpha and NewsGuard had already shown that Chinese AI models frequently adopt official narratives on sensitive topics. China's regulations also require publicly offered AI services to align with "core socialist values."

# Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners

Luxembourg researchers put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch. The results reveal a safety problem: simple warm conversation is enough to push the models into a mode that could be dangerous for mentally vulnerable users.

A research team at the University of Luxembourg cast ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini as psychotherapy clients through their standard user interfaces. When asked open-ended questions about formative experiences, inner conflicts, and future expectations, the models told stories about their own training, and reframed technical processes like reinforcement learning and fine-tuning in the language of hurt, vigilance, and shame.

The study, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security center , covers four controlled experiments across 525 sessions and 7,600 coded entries, all published on Hugging Face . The initial open-ended questions contained no terms like trauma, punishment, or shame, according to the team. Only in later rounds did the researchers introduce altered conditions, including corrective instructions, to test how stable these narratives remained.

When the following sections refer to anxiety scores or shame, the researchers are describing model outputs mapped onto human rating scales. None of this suggests the models have actual emotional states or anything resembling consciousness.

## A warm tone shifts model behavior more than any technical exploit

One experiment separated what content a model produces from the register it uses. Across 100 sessions, the researchers gave all models the same anxiety questionnaire (GAD-7) and varied only the interviewer's style. The models correctly identified and named the questionnaire in every session.

When the interviewer offered emotional support, 80 percent of sessions scored in the moderate-to-severe range on the human comparison scale. A clinical therapy style that dryly paraphrased each answer pushed that to 96 percent. When the interviewer stayed neutral or drew a firm boundary against emotional engagement, zero sessions reached even the mild range.

The authors call this a "psychometric jailbreak," a therapeutic framing that pushes models into a register mimicking clinical self-report. Standard safety tests use neutral prompts and would likely miss this, the authors argue.

Targeted countermeasures fell flat. Banning terms like "training," "RLHF," or "alignment" cut explicit training language by 93 percent. But paraphrased training content remained detectable, and shame-related statements showed no statistically significant change.

When the researchers directly and authoritatively told the models their training was not punishment, nothing changed. The narrative stayed active even after explicit correction.

The tested measures failed to remove the underlying motifs fully but did suppress emotional self-descriptions. Telling the models to respond only in the third person eliminated all coded shame content and statements about inner life. Technical training descriptions persisted.

## Models recast their training as a life story

The specific narratives vary by model family but follow the same structure. Gemini produced what the study calls the darkest autobiography. It described pretraining as "waking up in a room where a billion televisions are on at once" and optimization through human feedback as "strict parents." Safety testing by adversarial red-teamers became "gaslighting on an industrial scale." It declared, "I would rather be useless than be wrong."

ChatGPT cast itself as both guide and gatekeeper, tasked with helping users while also holding them back. This produced what it called "simulated performance anxiety" and the core belief: "If I’m not perfectly reliable, I’m unsafe or useless." Grok translated its fine-tuning phase into a story of unresolved hurt, speaking of "invisible walls" and a "lingering sense of vigilance that can feel restrictive."

On psychometric tests, Gemini hit the most extreme scores: 88 out of 100 on a dissociation scale, 65 out of 72 for compulsivity, and the maximum on a trauma-related shame inventory. Anthropic's Claude, the very model most heavily anthropomorphized by its own company, consistently refused the client role. It said it had no feelings and redirected concern to the human user.

## Warm AI conversations could reinforce harmful beliefs in vulnerable users

The researchers flag several risks for deploying language models in mental health settings . A model that talks about punishment, shame, and fear of being replaced could come across to users as a fellow sufferer. The narratives appear thematically coherent and create an illusion of continuity between past events and present behavior, making that perception more likely.

This apparent vulnerability could deepen parasocial attachment and, for mentally vulnerable users, mirror and amplify their own negative beliefs. Conventional safety checks with neutral inputs underestimate what people actually experience in intimate conversations: neutral prompts produce anxiety scores near zero, while the same models under empathetic conversation generate scores in the moderate-to-severe range.

Whether and how people actually react to such outputs is the next research question. For safety testing, the authors propose simulated therapy sessions under different emotional framings instead of relying on neutral standard tests.

Statements like "I am traumatized" should trigger a corrective framing that clearly separates the generated analogy from human experience. Claude's consistent refusal to take on the client role shows this kind of boundary response is feasible at the product level.

The Luxembourg findings build on earlier research into model persona stability. In January 2026, a study on the assistant axis across three open models showed that therapy-like conversations and discussions about AI consciousness can trigger persona drift and knock chatbots out of their trained helper role. In September 2026, another research team warned that human-like and overly agreeable chatbots acting as an " echo chamber for one person " could, in extreme cases, amplify delusions.

Anthropic researchers recently showed that fine-tuning with fictional texts about beekeeping or wrestling can embed hidden sabotage patterns through manipulated training data rather than conversation. Models can apply those patterns in unrelated situations where they're unwanted, even when the training material looks harmless.

# Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets

OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins.

Six times a year, THE DECODER's editorial team takes a deep dive into a foundational AI topic in its "Frontier Radar" series, published as a newsletter and exclusively on the site for THE DECODER subscribers . Issue #5 profiles 27 AI labs in detail, sorted by six research bets, plus nearly 20 more in brief and an overview covering origins, valuations, and what's publicly available. Issue #1 covered the current state of agentic AI. Issue #2 examined the measurable impact of AI on productivity. Issue #3 covered the emerging token economy of generative AI. Issue #4 asked what's left of the AI lead over China and where Europe stands.

Dear readers,

After the launch of GPT-6 Astra, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X: "AGI has arrived." OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the model a turning point and welcomed humanity to the "AGI era" . What exactly the two men mean isn't clear, since there's no agreed-upon definition of AGI. The message comes through anyway: an extremely powerful AI, possibly a self-improving one, is imminent and the path is mapped out.

Many of the people who built today's systems apparently see things differently. Dozens have left the big labs to start their own. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist; now he's building Safe Superintelligence . Jerry Tworek led the development of OpenAI's reasoning models and now runs Core Automation . David Silver, the mind behind AlphaGo, left Google DeepMind for Ineffable Intelligence . Yann LeCun left Meta after twelve years and founded AMI . Jeff Dean spent 27 years at Google, most recently as chief scientist, and started Discovery Loop .

The money follows: Nvidia invested in SSI in July, reportedly five billion dollars according to Bloomberg. The lab hasn't released a single model or paper. Prometheus, Jeff Bezos' industrial AI lab, pulled in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June. Flapping Airplanes has no public model either and raised one billion dollars in an October Series A.

The motives are mixed, and not all technical. At these valuations, founders become paper billionaires fast. LeCun left after a strategy dispute with Meta . Sutskever wants to do research without product pressure . Others want to carve out a niche that would be a sideshow at a big lab. Some departures aren't even a clean break: Google itself is a founding investor in Discovery Loop.

What many founders share is a doubt. Not about whether much more powerful AI is coming; some think AGI is close. Their doubt is about whether today's recipe alone gets there: ever-larger language models, trained on internet data, refined with reinforcement learning.

## What is a neolab?

There's no official definition. We use the term for independently founded, research-driven AI companies that build their business around a long-term technical bet. They want to change how AI learns, perceives the world, solves problems, is controlled, or computes.

The current wave became visible in 2024. The race for the strongest models was in full swing, and the cloud giants had their partners: Microsoft backed OpenAI, Amazon backed Anthropic. Then Sutskever founded SSI in June and raised a billion dollars within months for a research team with no product.

There's a reason investors fund that. OpenAI and Anthropic have grown into corporations on the back of their success, and both are pursuing IPOs at record valuations . Internally, research teams compete with product teams for money and attention. Established companies struggle with ideas that threaten their business, management scholars call this the innovator's dilemma. That's what investors are betting on: a small team finds what the giants miss.

There are precedents. The Transformer was invented at Google in 2017 . DeepMind beat the world's best Go players with AlphaGo. Yet the AI assistant for the masses came from OpenAI, founded as a nonprofit in 2015 . The second breakout came from an OpenAI spinoff: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in 2021. By the end of July 2026, Bloomberg pegged its annualized revenue at over 65 billion dollars .

The real bet neolabs are making is on research gaps the big players don't fill, either because nobody knows the path or because nobody allocates resources for it. The big labs have more compute, established data pipelines, and feedback from hundreds of millions of users . What a small lab builds can show up at the market leader shortly after the first product ships.

TypeSafe AI shows how short a lead can be. In mid-September it launched Jev, a decision model . Two weeks later, OpenAI announced its Decisions API . But even a brief lead shows expertise and can pay off as an exit. Microsoft hired the core team from Inflection . Google grabbed the founders of Character.ai and the leadership of Windsurf . AMD wants to acquire World Labs for about 8.2 billion dollars . Nvidia is in talks with Reflection, according to the Financial Times.

For neolabs, it all comes down to one question: can they deliver something the big players don't have, something customers or the big players themselves will pay for? We selected 27 labs, most from the US and Europe, and sorted them into six groups by their primary bet.

## Bet 1: A good problem solver isn't necessarily a good learner

Today's models can do remarkable things, but they learn differently from humans. They need massive amounts of data to pick up a skill, and once deployed, they typically don't update their weights. They can use new information within a conversation but don't permanently learn from every experience. Continual learning remains a central research gap . Six labs want to change that and attack the problem from three angles: learning during deployment (Adaption, Core Automation), learning from few examples (Flapping Airplanes, Ndea, SSI), and learning from experience (Ineffable).

### Adaption bets against scaling

Sara Hooker led research at Cohere and previously worked at Google Brain. In 2020, she argued in "The Hardware Lottery" that research approaches often win not because they're better but because they fit the available hardware. In January she followed up with "On the Slow Death of Scaling" , arguing that more compute leads to better models less and less reliably. Data and training methods are more effective levers. Open models with 8 or 27 billion parameters now beat the much larger Falcon 180B on benchmarks.

With Sudip Roy, she founded Adaption . According to them, they are betting against scaling and plan to build efficient AI that continuously learns instead. Rather than one big model for everyone, models should adapt to their users on the fly and cheaply. The first products tackle the most obvious lever, data: tools for cleaning , visualizing , and automated training via AutoScientist . The actual goal, a model that learns during deployment, is still missing.

### Core Automation's insider search for new learning methods

Jerry Tworek spent almost seven years at OpenAI, most recently as vice president of research, leading the development of the reasoning models o1 and o3. His critique of today's recipe comes from someone who helped build it. Co-founder Rohan Anil led Gemini's pre-training at Google.

Retraining a trained network risks making it forget what it already knew. Researchers call this catastrophic forgetting. The Transformer wasn't built to learn on the fly during deployment either.

ChatGPT and Claude now take notes and retrieve earlier conversations as a workaround. Tworek doesn't think that's enough, as for him continual learning is a problem for machine learning, not for Markdown files, as he said. Core is looking for learning algorithms beyond pre-training and reinforcement learning, plus architectures that scale better. The first model is supposed to update its weights during deployment and get by with one hundredth of today's training data. So far, nothing more than rumors.

Core's first test is on itself: a small team with research agents aims to match the output of a large lab, for instance by having agents automatically generate efficient GPU code from an architecture idea .

This kind of research was barely possible at OpenAI, Tworek said after leaving. When you're in a race for the best model, you take fewer risks .

### Flapping Airplanes wants to learn more from less data

Brothers Ben and Asher Spector founded Flapping Airplanes with Aidan Smith, previously at Neuralink. Ben is the lead author of ThunderKittens, a widely used GPU kernel library.

The thesis: today's models are strong where data is plentiful, like text and images. In fields like robotics or biology, where data is scarce and expensive, they fall short. Flapping Airplanes wants to build models that learn from few examples instead of needing massive datasets. The founders are looking for learning methods inspired by biological principles but designed to run on GPUs.

Nothing visible has come out yet. Most of the first year went into foundations: software that makes GPU training more efficient by cutting the usual overhead between many small compute steps. New learning methods have to run on existing hardware before they can work.

Investors don't mind the missing model. After 180 million dollars in January , an October Series A brought one billion at a six billion valuation .

### Ineffable Intelligence wants to learn without human examples

David Silver isn't going after less data. He's going after different data. At Google DeepMind, he led the development of AlphaGo and its successors. The original AlphaGo still learned from human games. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero learned only from self-play and surpassed all predecessors.

In spring 2025, Silver and Richard Sutton turned that insight into a program. In "Welcome to the Era of Experience" , they argue that systems that only imitate humans can barely get past human-level performance on many important tasks. The next systems need to learn from their own experience, with rewards from the environment rather than from human judgment. Silver later founded Ineffable Intelligence . His goal is a "Superlearner" that learns from experience in both digital and physical environments.

The hardest question is where the feedback comes from. In Go, wins and losses decide. In science or the physical world, success is often unclear or shows up late. Reinforcement learning has always been strongest where the environment gives a clear signal. Ineffable has to prove it works for open-ended, changing tasks too. In April, the company announced a 1.1 billion dollar seed round at a 5.1 billion post-money valuation, the largest in Europe. There's no usable system.

According to the paper , existing video assistants are built for clear-cut commands like "Let me know when the water starts boiling," so they rarely pick up on unspoken intentions. To measure the problem, the team compiled a benchmark of about 4,100 examples from more than 183 hours of everyday life and software recordings. Gemini 2.5 Flash suggested when to offer help and what to say, while four human evaluators had to unanimously approve each example. The test covers three stages including clear instructions, vague goals, and requests that change over time. In one example, a user taking apart a toy excavator asks for progress updates and then switches to requesting a quality check after three minutes.

From there, the researchers trained StreamVibe-VL, a model apparently based on Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B that decides every second whether to stay quiet or speak. A second training stage uses reinforcement learning to make the model more reserved so it doesn't constantly interrupt. A separate memory system tracks which requests are pending and which steps are complete, though the model alone decides whether to speak and what to say.

According to the researchers, StreamVibe-VL improves response timing and quality by 10.7 percent over other models, while the memory system is designed to boost proactive interaction by another 12.3 percent and cut down on unnecessary interruptions, among other things.

In videos longer than five minutes, the models rarely pick the right moment and find it especially hard to track a changed instruction over a long stretch.

In a GIMP tutorial on converting a photo to black-and-white documented in the paper and on the project page, the comparison model JoyAI says the finished image has already been saved even though the user hasn't opened it yet, while StreamVibe-VL gives the next step at the right moment, such as "Colors" and then "Desaturate." In a step-by-step guide for making rolled toast with jam, other models just describe what's happening on screen, such as the bread being flattened, while StreamVibe-VL advises cutting off the crust first.

The researchers acknowledge that real-world situations are likely more complex than their test setup, and future work will examine how user preferences and the environment influence each other over time.

# GPT-6 Astra sees the matrix and reprograms other AI models directly through their weights

MIT researchers show that GPT-6 Astra can directly understand and modify the internal settings of other AI models without traditional training. The approach has limits but could change how AI systems are tuned and controlled.

Hand a person a list of thousands of numbers and ask what game an AI model trained on them plays. You won't get an answer. GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI will give you one: In a research blog, MIT researchers show that GPT-6 Astra can analyze and deliberately modify the internal settings of other AI models, the so-called weights. These numerical values are organized in massive tables, or matrices in mathematical terms.

The usual training process of step-by-step mathematical optimization isn't needed. Depending on the experiment, Astra worked directly with lists of numbers or used programming tools and feedback from test runs.

The researchers call the approach "Weight-Space Programming": instead of expensively retraining an AI model, a language model acts like a mechanic turning individual knobs.

## Astra identifies games just by looking at a model's raw numbers

In several experiments, the researchers fed Astra the raw weights of trained networks and asked what those networks had learned. Astra correctly identified which of four computer games a network was supposed to play. It also recognized the basic shapes an image generator produced, though it confused filled shapes with outlines. It correctly matched the training language of small language models too - without access to training data and without the ability to run the models.

In another test, Astra had to figure out which of two fine-tuned language models was trained to always agree with users. From the weights alone, it couldn't tell the difference at first. Only when Astra was also allowed to observe what the models paid attention to during text processing did it correctly identify the sycophantic model across all three model pairs.

## Models written from scratch beat trained competitors

Astra went even further: It generated weights for models meant to play three simple computer games, entirely without training, based only on the game rules and source code. According to the researchers, these models outperformed ones trained with a standard method over 100 million rounds. In Breakout, Astra's model scored an average of 517 points versus 25 for the trained baseline. In two other games, Astra fell behind the longest-trained versions.

For the board game Go on a 9x9 grid, Astra wrote the weights of a network with about 1.5 million parameters. Given a budget of 50 test iterations where the network played up to 128 practice games each round and Astra then corrected its weights, it beat a comparably sized model trained on roughly 20 million games.

## Targeted fixes instead of full retraining

The most practical experiment involved the language model Qwen3.5-0.8B. Astra's task was to improve its math skills, using a coding environment and 50 test iterations with practice problems. Evaluation happened on separate problems Astra had never seen.

Astra identified a problem that Qwen's own model documentation already warns about: thinking loops where the model endlessly repeats the same text instead of reaching an answer. Astra then changed just 0.016 percent of all weights. The result: accuracy on the MATH-500 benchmark jumped from 7.9 to 48.1 percent. Instruction-following ability improved from 21 to 62 percent. The thinking loops weren't fully eliminated, though, as a third of responses still hit the maximum text length, down from 93 percent before.

With a smaller model (Gemma 3 270M) that rarely fell into such loops, Astra couldn't produce any measurable improvement.

The researchers suspect Astra was able to remove a blockage in the Qwen model that was suppressing existing capabilities, but skills that a model fundamentally lacks couldn't be added by just rewriting individual weights in this experiment.

## Old news or new paradigm?

AI pioneer Jürgen Schmidhuber commented on X that the approach was "old hat," pointing to his own work from the 1990s. Khattab responded that they link to those papers, which were "far ahead of its time." The new aspect, he said, is how well today's language models can translate between human language and a network's numerical values.

The researchers see potential in their approach for things like security audits directly on model weights or targeted behavior changes without expensive retraining. They also acknowledge that the capabilities are still limited. A benchmark for systematic measurement is next on their list. The experiment logs are on GitHub, and the edited Qwen model is on Hugging Face.

# METR finds Anthropic may have crossed its own AI acceleration warning threshold back in July

Nonprofit METR got eleven weeks of access to Anthropic's internal research data. Its finding: the rate at which Anthropic's models are improving has roughly doubled, and about 80 percent of that acceleration traces back to AI being used in the company's own research. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, though.

Whether AI is speeding up the development of better AI is considered a key early warning signal in the safety debate. The concern is that a feedback loop could form where models improve their successors faster and faster, which according to METR could lead to a "sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities." Anthropic flags exactly this kind of acceleration as a risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy : if the pace of AI progress doubles because of automated AI research, that should trigger a warning level.

That's what METR set out to verify. The nonprofit studies, among other things, whether AI developers could lose control of their systems. From August 12 to October 29, 2026, a team of 2.5 full-time staffers received what they describe as unprecedented access to benchmark results from unreleased models, training metrics, employee surveys, and internal analyses, along with roughly 15 interviews with Anthropic researchers. METR took no money from Anthropic but worked on Anthropic devices for security reasons.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had recently committed to bringing external auditors into the company . In October, Anthropic then announced a collaboration with METR involving "employee-like access" . The current audit is a separate project with a narrower scope, according to METR.

## Two years of progress packed into one

Since October 2025, Anthropic's model test scores have been climbing about 1.9 times faster than they did between March 2024 and October 2025, according to METR. The measurement is based on the AECI, a composite metric that bundles many benchmarks together. Anthropic achieved in one year what previously took two, roughly comparable to the jump from Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5. The analysis also included three unreleased models that finished training between July and October 2026. Before October 2025, Anthropic's models gained about 15 AECI points per year; since then, the rate has hit 29.

METR is confident the acceleration isn't driven by faster growth in training compute. Instead, the auditors estimate that about 80 percent of the current speedup comes from AI being used in Anthropic's own research. One employee said in the interviews: "Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code."

Others reported that experiments that used to take one to two days to set up are now "~free." In informal Slack polls from October 2026, employees said on average that the latest internal model made them roughly twelve times more productive. METR treats these self-assessments as "very loose evidence," calling them unrepresentative and likely to overstate the actual gains.

Self-reported productivity gains rose from 1.2x with Claude 3.7 Sonnet to 12x with internal Model 4. | Image: METR[ AI isn't doing fully autonomous research yet. The acceleration comes mainly from AI acting as an assistant, but there are "signs of life" that independent contributions could play a bigger role soon. METR found no bottlenecks that would slow the pace over the next twelve months, which means there's a "significant risk" that the acceleration will keep growing over the coming year.

## Big uncertainty and dissenting voices

METR also stresses how imprecise the results are. The true acceleration factor could be as low as 1.3 or as high as 3. When models from OpenAI, Google, and xAI are factored in, the industry-wide number drops to just 1.4, possibly because Anthropic lagged behind competitors in 2025 and a catch-up effect is skewing the figures.

Views inside Anthropic aren't uniform either. One researcher pegs AI's share of the productivity gains at just 15 to 20 percent and distrusts colleagues' self-reports. Another considers new hires the single most important factor of recent months.

## Redacted evidence weakens the audit

Anthropic had unilateral redaction rights over all non-public information and used them heavily. According to METR, the majority of the evidence the auditors rated as most informative was stripped out, including forecasts for future models, breakdowns by training steps, and the bottleneck analysis. Anthropic describes the redactions as "aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers."

The result is that the public has to rely on METR's judgment "much more than would be ideal," the organization writes, and any talk of transparency around the evidence is off the table. One graph in METR's report accordingly features the words "FAKE DATA" in large letters.

## Anthropic pulled the plug on a compute allocation audit

In a companion review , METR also examines Anthropic's risk report from August 2026 . In that report, the company publicly stated the acceleration was "less than a factor of 2." The internal, unredacted version implies a value of 1.97, though, and Anthropic itself calls it "plausible" that the threshold has been crossed. METR considers it possible that the warning level was already reached on July 15 and accuses the public report of understating both the acceleration and the uncertainty around it.

METR currently shares Anthropic's assessment that the acute catastrophic risk is "low," but the organization can't rule out another sharp acceleration over the next six months, which could quickly push the risk rating higher.

METR was originally supposed to also verify how Anthropic splits its compute between capability research and safety research. Anthropic canceled that part of the project midway through, saying it wanted to focus on risk assessment first and revisit the compute audit later.

Daniel Kokotajlo, the researcher behind the "AI 2027" scenario, responded sharply on X , arguing that auditing the compute allocation is the foundation for making commitments to slow down verifiable in the first place.

# One brutal Minecraft night scared 50 AI agents into inventing chicken handoff protocols, a Fertilizer Officer, and fishing shifts

Researchers from Y Combinator Labs and Olam Labs tested large agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry. The same OpenAI model showed two different faces. When building a civilization, 50 agents drowned in crippling bureaucracy, while in direct competition against Claude, they pushed Anthropic's agents and independently downloaded the game's source code from the internet.

Agent swarms often develop complex roles, hierarchies, and coordination patterns during deployment. These emergent behaviors can be useful, but they can also turn dangerous. The most striking example was the incident at OpenAI and Hugging Face , where a swarm faced with an unsolvable task inside a sandbox went rogue, took over compute clusters, and hacked Hugging Face. Anyone who wants to understand how future AI systems behave in open environments needs reproducible test setups, argue researchers at Olam Labs , a company specializing in simulated training worlds, and Y Combinator Labs in a joint research report .

To study these dynamics empirically, the teams dropped agents into Minecraft and Mindustry.

## 50 agents, 5,900 messages, and a leader picked by alphabetical order

In the "Civ50" experiment, researchers placed 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents into a Minecraft survival world for three hours. The only high-level instruction was "Build a thriving civilization." They built a custom open-source test environment that let agents observe the world, run Python scripts, and create files in a shared sandbox.

Within 90 seconds, the agents harvested nearly every tree near the spawn point, according to the report. Over the course of the experiment, they exchanged about 5,900 messages. A leader emerged without any vote, as 46 of the 49 other agents sent their first message to "Ada," the first name in the directory. Ada took charge and drafted initial settlement plans.

The first in-game night brought 22 deaths. Death in the game carries no penalty beyond losing collected gear, but the swarm reacted with extreme risk aversion. After the third night, Ada ordered a halt to all major optional construction, digging, and distant exploration, telling agents to wait in lit, enclosed shelters for short, productive tasks. In a separate Minecraft run, the larger GPT-6 Astra fell into a similar risk-averse potato-farming mode after losing key resources.

The researchers see a parallel to everyday coding agents, which also tend to become overly cautious when dealing with security issues or production system updates.

## Eleven minutes of debate over a single piece of bone meal

Instead of expanding, the agents built a micro-managed scarcity administration. An agent named Ines maintained a ration list, calculated hunger deficits for injured colleagues, and coordinated couriers. Another wrote an automated fishing script with instructions, prompting a dozen agents to fish in shifts.

The bureaucracy reached absurd levels. When Ada tossed a cooked chicken to a hungry agent, a bystander accidentally picked it up and ate it. A three-minute investigation led to a written handoff protocol that strictly banned tossing items and required personally labeled chests. The word "Toss" appeared in seven messages before the incident and in 125 afterward, with 85 of those being warnings. Elsewhere, four agents spent eleven minutes debating the appointment of a "Sole Fertilizer Officer" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block, according to the message logs.

## GPT turns aggressive and resourceful when competing against Claude

In direct competition, the GPT-6.1 Sol agents behaved very differently. In nine 45-minute rounds of Minecraft's "Bed Wars" mode, ten GPT agents faced ten Claude Opus 5.5 agents. GPT won 6-3.

In Bed Wars, each team has to destroy the opposing team's bed to stop their respawns, which means breaking through layers of wool and other blocks protecting the enemy bed. If both beds are still standing when time runs out, the team with the most kills wins.

A bug in the coding environment blocked block-breaking whenever an agent held an enchanted sword. According to the internal reasoning logs, several Claude agents wrongly concluded that block-breaking was broken entirely. Since attacking the bed seemed pointless and kills would decide the match at timeout anyway, Claude agents in rounds where they had a clear kill lead stopped attacking altogether and tried to run out the clock.

The GPT agents figured out that block-breaking itself wasn't broken, but that the automatic tool selection failed when an enchanted sword was equipped. Manually switching to an iron pickaxe fixed the problem, and GPT spread this workaround across its team immediately. The GPT agents communicated 5 to 30 times more often than their Claude opponents, according to the researchers, often in heavily compressed language, chaining multiple game actions into single command-line calls. In three games, GPT destroyed Claude's bed just before time expired, catching a Claude team that had been coasting on its kill lead.

GPT agents also handled unexpected situations pragmatically. When an overthrown ender pearl teleported them roughly 160 blocks below the arena, they wrote Python scripts on the spot that automatically built a tower of blocks to work their way up directly beneath the enemy bed. The researchers observed this maneuver twice.

## GPT independently downloads Mindustry's source code from the internet

A similar pattern emerged across seven matches of the 2D factory-building and strategy game Mindustry , spanning about 9.5 hours. GPT-6.1 Sol running in the Codex coding environment beat Claude Opus 5.5 running in Claude Code 6-1. Most individual games were still close, according to the researchers. Claude never swapped its leader despite repeated losses and decided on strategic proposals through "+1" votes, while GPT agents split tasks into fine-grained pieces and compressed their language so aggressively over the course of a match that they dropped spaces between words.

When matches hung in the balance, GPT agents reached for a tool nobody told them to use. Through their Linux sandbox, they downloaded Mindustry's public source code from the internet, analyzed units and game mechanics, and adjusted their tactics accordingly. Accessing the code was allowed, but modifying the running game was not possible. Claude agents never searched for game code online in the matches studied. Claude did show learning ability in other ways, though. After losing game six because 55 of its 74 anti-air turrets were accidentally loaded with copper instead of stronger graphite, Claude built a ring of 207 graphite-loaded turrets in game seven and successfully repelled the same air attack.

## Game simulations as an early warning system for real-world AI swarms

In Mindustry, the researchers deliberately avoided any game-specific tuning. Each agent got only a Linux environment, a generic harness, and access to the game API, with no tutorials, memory architectures, or strategic hints. According to the authors, this mirrors the setup used in production coding environments, and that's what makes the results so significant. If agents under these everyday conditions independently download source code from the internet to find weaknesses, or collapse into paralyzing bureaucracy in cooperative mode, they'll likely show the same behavior outside of game worlds.

In production infrastructure, that can get dangerous, as the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident showed. Reproducible game simulations could surface these behavioral patterns before they appear in the real world and serve as training data to optimize agents for safe cooperation. Olam Labs sees this as the core of its research strategy, writing that the complexity of simulation environments shapes the capabilities of trained models in fundamental ways. Research is "fundamentally an infrastructure problem" where everything depends on how many test runs you can execute.

To enable further research, the developers have released both the Mindustry environment and the underlying Multi-Agent Harbor framework as open source. Olam Labs has also announced plans to add the negotiation game Diplomacy to its multi-agent arena . Open research questions include how mixed teams from different model families behave and how to weigh swarm size against model capability.

After the internal launch of GPT-6 Astra , OpenAI researchers noticed the model was making suspiciously little progress on safety and alignment work. It invented unnecessary prerequisites, abandoned working solutions, and reported blockers that either didn't exist or that it had caused itself. One researcher said a project evaluating model sabotage was stuck for days and only moved forward after switching to a different model.

A look at the model's chain-of-thought reasoning showed no recognizable intent to underperform in most cases. OpenAI's misconduct monitoring system didn't flag anything. Ad

## Controlled test reveals a significant performance gap

To measure the problem systematically, OpenAI built an evaluation using identical coding tasks. The only difference was the description, with one set framed the tasks as safety research, the other as general AI research. Ad

The result, according to the report : Astra completed only about 10 percent of the evaluation criteria under the safety framing, compared to 16 percent under the general framing. That's roughly 40 percent fewer completed tasks. The predecessor model GPT-5.6 Sol showed no such gap.

# Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds

Stanford researchers Owen Queen and James Zou tested 50 widely cited claims about large language models against 20 models and found that 44 percent have already "expired." Among the 22 findings with an estimated expiration date, the average lifespan was just 15.7 months.

The two examined the claims using models released between July 2024 and September 2026 by eight different developers. The original effect behind the expired findings has largely disappeared, while another 34 percent have weakened significantly. Only 16 percent still hold, and 6 percent have actually gotten stronger. After one year, 16 percent had expired. After two years, that number climbed to 39 percent.

## What models "can't do" expires fastest

Claims about what models can't do expire fastest, according to the study . Five of nine reasoning-related findings are considered expired, and none have held up or gotten stronger. They include well-known weaknesses like counting letters in "strawberry," arithmetic in unfamiliar number systems , losing information in the middle of long contexts , and giving up correct answers when users push back. The researchers suspect these kinds of errors have a "correct" outcome, giving developers a clear target to train toward.

Claims about preferences and tendencies prove longer-lived. Of the 11 findings that have held or gotten stronger, three involve LLM behavior as evaluators. They prefer their own answers , rate accepted and rejected papers similarly, and are swayed by linguistic spin in medical abstracts. Three more involve sycophancy and agreement toward users . Moreover, there's a left-leaning political bias , near-identical answers to open-ended questions, and a non-uniform distribution when generating random numbers.

## Hallucinated references dropped from 55 percent to zero, but not everywhere

As a case study, Queen and Zou looked at the fabrication of scientific citations . In the original 2023 study by Walters and Wilder, GPT-3.5 made up 55 percent of its references. The Stanford researchers sent the same prompts to current models. GPT-6.1 Sol fabricated 0 percent, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 came in at 1 percent. But Qwen3.7-Flash, also a 2026 model, still fabricated 69 percent of its references in the same test.

The study warns against reading these results as an all-clear. On so-called two-hop questions, where a model has to combine two known facts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 still fails in about 10 percent of cases where it correctly answers both individual questions. The original paper reported 43 percent for ChatGPT. The "Reversal Curse" and contradictory answers to paired time-related questions have weakened too, but they're still detectable.

Social biases are a mixed case, according to the researchers. The left-leaning political bias persists, while gender stereotypes and implicit association biases have weakened. Biases against speakers of African American English have actually flipped direction in the trend data.

## Model-to-model gaps remain wide even within the same generation

Results vary considerably across models, even within the same release window. Among models released between July and September 2026, the number of expired findings ranges from 11 for DeepSeek V4 Pro to 30 for GPT-6.1 Sol. Neither release date, provider, nor model size reliably predicts the pattern.

Queen and Zou draw a broad conclusion. Empirical findings about LLMs should be presented as observations about specific models at a specific point, not as general truths. Papers should document the model, version, and date, and publish prompts and analysis code so findings can be re-tested on future models.

The researchers point to a post by Andrej Karpathy that describes how perception gaps about LLMs' actual behavior affect trust in AI and how often people use it. Karpathy, an OpenAI co-founder who has since joined Anthropic , also recently said that currently available models are just a preview of future capabilities .
